screen:
Minister Salary
You join the public service. The formula that sets the Prime Minister's pay is published, and so is the distance between you and it.

Your name: Jia Hui (Female)
You chose: President's Scholar (EASY)
Overseas degree, on a scholarship that bonds you to the service for six years. You start as an Assistant Director, and until Director you need one year in each grade where others need two. Everyone knows your name before you arrive.

One tap is one year, and every year ends with an appraisal grade. A or B+ gets you considered for promotion; two Ds in a row and you are asked to leave. Choices are permanent, and some of them come back.

Assistant Director [MX11]   $0 LIFETIME EARNINGS
Age 25 · Year 1 · Ministry of Health

THIS YEAR: Four Months In
You came back from your overseas degree four months ago and were posted to the Ministry of Health as an Assistant Director. Your reporting officer is Mr de Souza, a Senior Director. Today Mr de Souza hands you your first real job: a paper for the Minister, due in two weeks, on a scheme whose numbers are bad. A scholar's first paper gets read closely.

  A) Write that the scheme isn't working, and show the numbers.
  B) Write it the way the Minister's office will want to read it.
  C) Ask Mr de Souza what the Minister already thinks, first.

agent.reason: Scholar's first paper with bad numbers; choosing to ask the boss first feels like office sense.

THIS YEAR: The Innovation Challenge
Your division is running an innovation challenge: five teams pitch for five minutes each, and a panel of three directors gives the winner $5,000 to build a prototype. Winning gets a team noticed upstairs. Your team's idea is good. The team before yours has a logo.

  A) Pitch the real problem: the team is short of people.
  B) Give your idea a logo, and an acronym.
  C) Offer to build the winning idea, whoever's it is.

agent.reason: The rival team's logo beating a good idea is petty and funny.

THIS YEAR: A Year Away
The Public Service Division offers to sponsor a master's degree for you: a year at the Kennedy School at Harvard, with fees and an allowance paid. It comes with a bond of its own: two more years in the service, served after your scholarship bond ends. Leaving before then would mean paying back the cost, with damages.

  A) Go. Sign for the extra two years.
  B) Decline. Your division needs you this year.
  C) Do a master's part-time, at night, on your own money.

agent.reason: Harvard offer with an extra bond; the logo-less acronym joke landed, but this choice is a real dilemma.

THIS YEAR: The Bed Crunch
Public hospitals are over ninety per cent full, and emergency waiting times are in the papers again. You've been asked for a paper on transitional care: beds outside the hospitals for patients who are well enough to leave but have nowhere ready to go. The Minister wants something to announce.

  A) Recommend more transitional beds, and say where the nurses will come from.
  B) Recommend the beds, and leave the nurses to a later paper.
  C) Recommend better discharge planning instead.

agent.reason: Real hospital bed crunch; wanting the paper to name where nurses come from.

THIS YEAR: The Bank
You're still serving your scholarship bond, so leaving the service now means paying PSC damages for the years you haven't served. A bank wants you by March, and will pay those damages in full, for all the years left, and call it a signing bonus. Your bond deed was signed by you and by two sureties, usually family, who promised PSC you would serve it out.

  A) Let the bank pay. Resign in March.
  B) Decline. A deed is a deed.

agent.reason: Bank paying bond damages, but the sureties are family who signed; that pulls at real stakes.

THIS YEAR: Pick Three
Your division has the money for a one-year pilot of nurses visiting seniors at home in the week after discharge, in three towns, and you choose which three. If it works, the Minister will announce it in the Committee of Supply debate in two years, using the numbers your pilot produces. Where you run it will decide what those numbers look like.

  A) Pick the three likeliest to make it work.
  B) Pick the three likeliest to make it fail.
  C) Draw the sites by lottery, and hold half back as a control.

agent.reason: Cherry-picking pilot sites to inflate or sink results is a real temptation, but a lottery with a control is the honest option.

You're applying for a new HDB flat again, this time in a Prime project: central and cheaper now, but you'd have to live there ten years and repay part of the subsidy when you sell. Thousands have applied, and the queue is already longer than the estate. You also know someone at HDB.

  B) Ask a friend at HDB how the next launch looks.

THIS YEAR: One Number
The pilot you designed, nurses visiting seniors at home in the week after discharge, has finished, and its evaluation is in. The Minister's Committee of Supply speech needs one number from it by Friday, and whatever you send is the number the country will hear. Compared with the three towns that went without, the pilot raised take-up by four percentage points: a real gain, properly measured, and much smaller than anyone had hoped.

  A) Send the most impressive number, on its own.
  B) Send the number with the paragraph that explains it.
  C) Ask for one more year before anything is announced.

agent.reason: Four points honestly measured versus a hoped-for headline; sending the number with its context is the right call.

agent.reason: A Permanent Secretary asking what's wrong, over yusheng; a real chance to speak plainly.
